name: Calibration

claims.claim_text: Measurement calibration rests on a traceability chain in which instrument readings are compared back to national standards such as those held by NIST, so that widely separated instruments ultimately refer to the same small set of primary references.
claims.quote_verbatim: like even how they just compare it all back to NIST standards and stuff like that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A repeatable error can be calibrated out of a measurement, but uncertainty and drift cannot; they set the floor on how much confidence a measurement can carry.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can always calibrate out error. But uncertainty, then you just start
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Precision instrumentation destined for extreme field environments is fully insulated so that large swings in ambient temperature do not disturb the calibrated internals.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's the reason they insulate it, right? Yeah, that's the reason it's fully insulated.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Melbourne, Hackerspace & Calibration - Vacuuous Vortex Verification

claims.claim_text: Freight shipping subjects calibrated equipment to heat cycling and shock, so high-accuracy standards are moved by dedicated truck rather than by ordinary carriers.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's just, shipping is not the way to do it with tailed equipment, right? I mean, that's the reason for the truck.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Melbourne, Hackerspace & Calibration - Vacuuous Vortex Verification

claims.claim_text: Agilent's Melbourne facility is a standards-grade calibration laboratory that receives instruments from overseas, including from the United States, for calibration; few laboratories at that level remain worldwide.
claims.quote_verbatim: And a lot of calibration gear from overseas is shipped to the Melbourne Lab to get calibrated.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Melbourne, Hackerspace & Calibration - Vacuuous Vortex Verification

claims.claim_text: Manual alignment procedures historically depended on tacit operator skill, with individual technicians known for knowing exactly how far to turn each adjustment, which makes such processes hard to transfer or scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've heard stories about the magic technician who knew just how many turns to go
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hamvention, Arduino and Intel - Burdensome Background Battology

claims.claim_text: Hand-assembly steps such as bonding optical parts with adhesive introduce unit-to-unit dimensional variation, which forces a per-unit calibration step that a dimensionally stable production design could avoid.
claims.quote_verbatim: There is a calibration process that we go through here, but that's because we hot glue all of them together.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: Specifying an expensive absolute-tolerance precision resistor instead of a cheap resistor plus a trimpot amounts to paying not to calibrate: the part price buys away the labor, time and error of a per-unit trim.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're paying for not calibrating at that point, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Motors And Upgrading Sinclairs - Adapting Apraxiated Automobiles

claims.claim_text: Small low-cost resistors drift substantially over time, so a value set by trimming a cheap part does not hold, whereas a precision part keeps its absolute value.
claims.quote_verbatim: And drift, because those little resistors drift like crazy.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Motors And Upgrading Sinclairs - Adapting Apraxiated Automobiles

claims.claim_text: The alternative to trimming each unit by hand is programmatic trim, which requires adding a DAC or programmable element plus all its supporting circuitry and firmware to an otherwise simple analog product.
claims.quote_verbatim: it would be putting a DAC on board and doing it programmatically, or putting a programmable system
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Motors And Upgrading Sinclairs - Adapting Apraxiated Automobiles

claims.claim_text: Production test on a low-cost precision product can be reduced from a full calibration to an automated pass-fail verification at a spot value, confirming each unit meets spec without characterizing it over the full range.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's like a spot value. Right. It's a verify.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Manufacturing By Wire And Skipping Testing - Calefacient Cuculine Cash

claims.claim_text: Calibration is valuable because it lets a design correct nonlinearities and reach precision the raw hardware does not have, but it adds a fragile, labor-intensive stage to production.
claims.quote_verbatim: They help you optimize for nonlinearities and all that other stuff and precision things.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Manufacturing By Wire And Skipping Testing - Calefacient Cuculine Cash

claims.claim_text: A shipment of resistors supplied at 1% tolerance in place of the specified 0.1% produced roughly a 50% failure rate in production test; a tolerance error large enough to move yield that far is obvious, whereas a 5% shift could be written off as noise.
claims.quote_verbatim: They were 1% tolerance instead of 0.1%
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Manufacturing By Wire And Skipping Testing - Calefacient Cuculine Cash

claims.claim_text: A low-drift-plus-software-calibration approach lets a design use inexpensive analog parts, since a unit that must be calibrated anyway gains nothing from parts that are accurate straight out of manufacture; what matters is that the parts stay stable after the calibration.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm happier with a low drift and fix it in software approach
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: Building accuracy into the hardware instead of into software calibration is expensive at the component level: individual precision shunt resistors in a hand-held current-measurement instrument cost about $5 each.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's why each one of my shunt resistors costs $5.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: Bench instruments are specified with a warm-up time before their accuracy claims hold, an assumption that fails for field instruments which are used at arbitrary times and temperatures and must therefore tolerate a wider range of operating conditions.
claims.quote_verbatim: you usually those respect for like warmup times and stuff like that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: Production calibration is a heavily statistical activity: gauge repeatability and reproducibility studies are run on test stands, stands are recalibrated on a schedule, and all results are tied back to a single traceable reference so that a stand going out of calibration can be detected.
claims.quote_verbatim: like gauge R&Rs that you make sure you're, you're, you know, if you have more than one stand, what happens if your stand goes out of cal?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Questioning Everyday Prototyping - Verrucose Vehicle Vitilitigation

claims.claim_text: USB 3.0 host implementations proved far less uniform across computers than USB 2.0, so instrument products relying on USB 3.0 face host-compatibility work in addition to their own analog and calibration software problems.
claims.quote_verbatim: USB 3.0 is not nearly as uniform and as well rolled out as USB 2.0 is
claims.speaker: Mark Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Recalibrating an instrument is best folded into scheduled maintenance, since work such as replacing aged capacitors already requires opening the instrument and disturbs its existing calibration.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you open it up and you need to like replace some caps, it's like, okay, well, you're halfway there. Now calibrate it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Calibrating analog components is straightforward for a handful of units but becomes a major manufacturing constraint at volume, since the per-unit time and equipment do not shrink with scale.
claims.quote_verbatim: if there's analog components and you have to do calibration, it's easy to do with a few units. But if you want to scale that, it becomes an issue
claims.speaker: Alvaro Prieto
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: Over-the-air firmware updates to a large fleet are staged rather than pushed at once, typically seeding roughly 0.1% of units first, then 1%, then 10%, so that a bad image is caught before it reaches the whole population.
claims.quote_verbatim: You have to give like 0.1% of the units, you know, start seeding the new firmware image.
claims.speaker: Alvaro Prieto
claims.episode_title: An interview with Alvaro and Jen from the URE Podcast

claims.claim_text: High-volume consumer products typically ship with a built-in self test rather than a full calibration, whereas a test-and-measurement manufacturer devotes a large share of its production engineering to the calibration setup itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: large scale consumer product might have like a built in self test, but you know, it's not going to get, it's not doing full calibration
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Calibrated instruments returned from a failed shipment cannot simply be forwarded to customers, because the units require recalibration and that capability may not exist at the seller's own site.
claims.quote_verbatim: they would have required a recalibration and I didn't want to send them out to people who ordered them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Ordinary shipping does not by itself invalidate an instrument's calibration; the temperature swings a package sees in transit are generally too small to shift a calibrated reading materially.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not like the calibration goes bad in shipping. I mean, there might be some temperature swings, but probably not enough for it to really matter.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Statistical process control on a calibration line tracks each test stand against the others, because two stands calibrating the same 10 mV range to the same nominal accuracy can sit offset from one another by a fraction of a percent.
claims.quote_verbatim: But then maybe the next test stand down does the same thing, but it's offset by 0.001%
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Because production test enforces a hard pass-fail limit, a unit sitting marginally outside the limit on one rig can pass on another rig whose offset runs the other way, which is why stand-to-stand agreement must be monitored rather than assumed.
claims.quote_verbatim: And you've always got hard limits. I mean, at some point you've got to manufacture a pass fail limit.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: In a home-built lithography stepper, focus is calibrated by pre-scoring the wafers with a laser cutter to give true indexing edges, focusing at each side of the wafer, and fitting the focus variation as a line in three-dimensional space that the computer then applies across the wafer.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then I can draw, I can draw a line in 3d space of how that focus changes and you can approximate it on the computer and it works.
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: When a positioning table has mechanical slop, every move must approach the target from the same side in X and Y so that backlash contributes a constant rather than a variable error; the amount of slop can be measured at different points of travel and compensated.
claims.quote_verbatim: if your table has slop in it, you'll have to approach from the same side every time when, in X and Y
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: A pick-and-place machine needs a machine-specific component library and calibration data for each component type, not just X-Y placement coordinates, because the head is a robot whose pick and placement behavior depends on the part geometry.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need like component libraries for each type of pick and place as well
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Introducing a component the assembly line has not run before remains a manual step, requiring an engineer to look up the datasheet and determine the part's physical dimensions before the machine can handle it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it still requires you looking up a data sheet and determining what size that component is
claims.speaker: Chris Denney

claims.claim_text: Even with the nozzle position calibrated exactly, reliable picking from tape depends on separately tuned parameters — how long the nozzle lingers on the part, how much suction is applied, and when vacuum is released — and these must be dialed in for each component type.
claims.quote_verbatim: do you have enough suction? Do you release at the right time?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Specification setting is an economic exercise: loosening a published spec by a tenth of a percent can permit a part that costs an order of magnitude less, and pushing calibration onto the user is another way of relaxing what the factory must guarantee.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I loosen my spec by 0.1%, I can use this part that's 10 times cheaper
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: CMOS used in space is not radiation hard, so spacecraft SOCs embed sensors that monitor bias, voltage and current conditions and detect when radiation has shifted the circuit away from its characterized operating point.
claims.quote_verbatim: the radiation has changed something. We need to calibrate.
claims.speaker: Adrian Tang

claims.claim_text: A space-grade RF synthesizer can carry hundreds of adjustment knobs — clock phase, bias conditions, clock and VCO tuning, output stage trim and output match — plus an integrated subprocessor that runs a calibration routine whenever a monitored parameter leaves its allowed corridor.
claims.quote_verbatim: There'd be an integrated subprocessor just doing calibration along with the RF circuits with RF sensors everywhere. And the moment something goes out of corridor, we activate that subprocessor.
claims.speaker: Adrian Tang

claims.claim_text: Extreme temperature excursions shift the operating point of spacecraft electronics in the same way radiation does, so on-board calibration must cover the thermal range as well as radiation-induced drift.
claims.quote_verbatim: Sometimes the chip gets very cold or very hot, and we need to calibrate for that.
claims.speaker: Adrian Tang

claims.claim_text: A common class of reported field failure is not a defective part but a calibration gap in the application: the device shows an offset or gain error of a few LSBs that is inside its published specification, while the customer's calibration scheme does not compensate for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: And their calibration doesn't compensate for that. But that's within spec of what the device is specified.
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: The most common cause of returned parts reported as defective is crystal oscillator startup failure traced to incorrect load capacitors on the crystal, which is a board design error rather than a silicon fault.
claims.quote_verbatim: crystals don't have the right load capacitors on them. And so the crystal doesn't start up
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: High-frequency RF connectors must be tightened with a torque wrench, because an incorrectly torqued connector invalidates the calibration and can shift the measurement by a decibel or two.
claims.quote_verbatim: your calibration is not valid because you're going to be out by a dB or two
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Standard SMA connectors are unsuitable for measurements at 10 GHz and above; specialized precision connectors are used instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: don't do SMA for 10 gig. That's bad.

claims.claim_text: Older analog high-current power modules are calibrated with trimmer potentiometers, while newer digital modules expose calibration through software menus, with DACs replacing the mechanical trimpots.
claims.quote_verbatim: So you have some trimmer potentiometers and stuff like that to, to adjust. And, uh, then you have the, the digital power modules and those also have some kind of calibration in, in the menus
claims.speaker: Fredrik Kensander
claims.episode_title: High Current Power Supplies with Fredrik Kensander

claims.claim_text: A precision instrument whose factory test flow includes touchy calibration stages constrains contract manufacturer selection, favoring a nearby shop with a consistently skilled operator over a cheaper or more distant one.
claims.quote_verbatim: a high-touch product that has a few calibration or factory test stages, including calibration, that are a little touchy
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Established instrument manufacturers run calibration in a temperature-controlled room staffed by dedicated calibration technicians who put each unit through its full cal cycle, an environment that is not normally available at a contract manufacturer.
claims.quote_verbatim: we had like a temperature-controlled room where there were a couple technicians or calibration experts that knew what they were doing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A vector network analyzer calibration works by measuring artifacts whose true values are known and correcting the readings to match; resolving impedance requires three known standards, conventionally an open, a short and a load.
claims.quote_verbatim: for vector analyzers, to do impedance, you need to have three true things. So we usually use an open, a short, and a load
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: Practical open and short calibration standards are physically offset from the reference plane, so an uncorrected trace traces an arc rather than collapsing to a point; naming them simply 'open' and 'short' rather than 'offset open' and 'offset short' has been a lasting source of user confusion.
claims.quote_verbatim: All of our opens and shorts are offset, so they all have a little arc.
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: Where a component's behavior is not repeatable, it is characterized over temperature so the correct correction factor can be selected for the temperature at which the measurement is made.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have to characterize it over temperature. When it's not repeatable, so we can know, okay, at this temperature, we should use this factor
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: Testing a 64-element base-station antenna array requires 64 cables to blind-mate connectors and 64 separate calibrations performed at the end of each cable, which is automated by a robot that attaches the open, short and load standards in turn.
claims.quote_verbatim: Then you have to do 64 sets of calibrations on the end of each of those cables. So they'll have a robot that'll hook up the open short loads to the ends of the cables.
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: Calibrating is not the first step in a network analyzer measurement, despite being the answer most users give; modern analyzers have been pre-calibrated at the factory well enough that useful first measurements can be made before any user calibration.
claims.quote_verbatim: everybody says calibrate. And no, that's quite a ways in the process
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: The recommended network analyzer sequence is to connect the device and take the measurement uncalibrated first, sanity-check the result for obvious errors such as a part hooked up backwards, adjust cables, connectors and adapters and wiggle the part to confirm stability, and only then spend time calibrating.
claims.quote_verbatim: So the first thing you do is you make all your measurements that you want to make without doing any calibration.
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: Test cables stretch and shrink as they heat and cool, and because the measurement depends on propagation time, that dimensional change moves the measured phase; calibration removes the error as long as the cable state stays constant afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: The cables inside, as they get hot and cold, they stretch and shrink and that moves your phase around.
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: The impedance traceability chain begins with a precision airline whose impedance is derived from its physical dimensions at NIST; that airline calibrates a system, which in turn calibrates the loads and resistors used in ordinary laboratory calibration kits.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have an airline at NIST that they measure and they say, yeah, this airline is this impedance. And then they use that to calibrate a system that then you use to calibrate your loads
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: Two distinct things are called calibration: instrument calibration, which verifies that the instrument meets all its published specifications and is what the cal sticker certifies, and open-short-load calibration, which is properly error correction of a particular measurement setup.
claims.quote_verbatim: When we talk about calibration from the instrument side, what we're saying is we've measured the instrument and we verified that it meets all the published specifications.
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: An instrument can be substantially out of its certified calibration and still yield a reasonable measurement once error correction is applied, because error correction references the measurement to known standards at the time of use.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can be pretty far out of cal and on an instrument and still have error correction, return it to a reasonable measurement.
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: Calibration rigor is tiered by consequence of error: aerospace and defense work keeps everything in calibration, runs daily calibrations and records every variation, cell-tower equipment is held to a looser standard, handsets looser still, and amateur radio work only as tight as the operator needs.
claims.quote_verbatim: You have to run your daily calibrations. You have to record any variation.
claims.speaker: Joel Dunsmore

claims.claim_text: A sensor bought pre-calibrated to a guaranteed specification and read out over a digital bus such as I2C can remove the need for a functional or calibration test on the production line, whereas testing an uncalibrated sensor in-line would require stimulus hardware such as a pressure chamber.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're getting a sensor from a manufacturer and it's already guaranteed to a spec, and then it's talking over I squared C, you might not be doing that functional test

claims.claim_text: Production line test tooling is scoped for fast, precise verification of each unit on the line with live feedback, not for design validation work such as thermal vacuum or shake-and-bake testing at a certification lab.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is not really built for design validation
claims.speaker: Pete Staples

claims.claim_text: Guaranteeing a product's specification all the way back to a NIST standard carries real cost, because the manufacturer must own and maintain its own calibrated reference instruments in the chain.
claims.quote_verbatim: Having it pass all the way back through to a NIST standard is like, yeah, there's a lot of, there's a lot of costs there

claims.claim_text: A precision current-measurement adapter reaches its published specification through parts rather than trimming: a single resistor on the board costs about $4 at volume against roughly $12 at single-piece price, so the accuracy specification is effectively bought in the bill of materials.
claims.quote_verbatim: Heck, one single resistor on there is four bucks, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Open-source hardware built with lower-precision substitute components does not meet the original design's specification, and the original is separately guaranteed by custom-built test gear that checks every unit against spec.
claims.quote_verbatim: they put lower precision parts on it and it's not the same spec
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Calibration and functional test of a precision instrument require expensive equipment that a normal contract manufacturer does not have, so the instrument maker must supply the test stand and the CM is chosen partly for its willingness to host it.
claims.quote_verbatim: a huge part is making sure that it is working correctly and calibrated. So that's expensive equipment that is not part of a normal CM
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Using previous-generation instruments to calibrate the next generation risks generational degradation, in which each batch inherits and compounds the error of the units that calibrated it; the fix is to keep a traceable calibrated multimeter in series in the test fixture so every generation is referenced to the same external standard.
claims.quote_verbatim: in order not to introduce generational degrade there is a least traceable calibrated multimeter in series so that we're using that to to calibrate the units
claims.speaker: Werner Johansson
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: A precision measurement product can be locked to specific parts — 0.05% resistors, single-source op-amps, and a resistor costing around $3 with no substitute — so that the usual contract-manufacturer practice of substituting equivalent parts is not available.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't substitute the parts in that, right? They're all precision. Like, you know, 0.05% resistors.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: In test and measurement, the barriers protecting incumbents are bespoke supply chains for precision components and test methodologies that competitors are unwilling or unable to reproduce, including the ability to calibrate to a recognized standard.
claims.quote_verbatim: The things that are keeping out competitors are, you know, bespoke supply chains
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: An open-source pick-and-place ships with as much machine configuration as possible baked into the firmware at boot, leaving the user a guided calibration walkthrough supported by video tutorials, because the number of adjustable settings on such a machine is otherwise overwhelming.
claims.quote_verbatim: we just walk you through the whole process of going through Cal
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: In a distributed sensor company the systems integration site handles over-the-air and chip test, calibration and basic performance characterization against spherical and canonical radar targets and first-principles physics, while a separate software site tests the same hardware against customer-facing performance metrics.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're testing against radar, spherical targets and canonical targets and first principles, testings and calibration
claims.speaker: Greg Charvat
claims.episode_title: The Terahertz Frontier with Greg Charvat of Teradar
